🔥🤖 8.64 s! TianGong Wins the 2026 Humanoid 100M Final! #robot #humanoidrobot #robotics  8.64 seconds... Another record broken. 🔥🔥🔥 The 100 m large-size final at the second World Humanoid Robot Games. TianGong (Tien Kung) Ultra took the title in 8.64, successfully defending its crown and once again running faster than the human world-record time of 9.58 seconds. 🥇 Gold — Tianjiao Team, TianGong Ultra — 8.64 s 🥈 Silver — Tianxiao Team, TianGong Ultra 🥉 Bronze — Honor, Lightning humanoid The record kept dropping throughout the Games, from 9.39 seconds on opening night to 8.86 in the semifinal and finally 8.64 in the final. For comparison, last year’s winning 100 m time was 21.50 seconds. And this year’s 100 m races are fully autonomous. Once the start command is given, the robots are on their own.

Chinese robotics company AheadForm unveiled one of its most lifelike humanoid robot faces at WAIC 2026 in Shanghai. Unlike most humanoid robot demonstrations that focus on walking, running, lifting objects, or performing acrobatic moves, AheadForm showcased highly realistic facial interaction. The robot features natural blinking, eye contact, synchronized speech, subtle head movements, and expressive facial reactions designed to make conversations feel more human. According to the company, its self-supervised AI and high-precision bionic actuation enable coordinated movements of the eyes, mouth, face, and speech, creating a remarkably lifelike communication experience. The result is a humanoid face realistic enough to make people take a second look. #robotics #artificialintelligence #humanoidrobot #waic2026 #technology

Chinese robotics company Unitree has unveiled the As2-W, a new wheel-legged robot that combines the speed of wheels with the flexibility of four legs. It automatically switches between driving and walking depending on the terrain. It can reach speeds of 21.6 km/h, travel over 30 km on a single charge, climb 45° slopes, clear 80 cm obstacles and handle stairs, gravel and other rough terrain. It’s also water and dust resistant and can operate in temperatures from -20°C to 55°C.  Unitree says it’s designed for everything from industrial inspections and cargo transport to research and outdoor exploration, making it a bridge between consumer and professional robotics.  #unitree #robotdog #robot #futuretech #chinatech

XPENG’s humanoid robot, known as IRON, represents the company’s expansion beyond electric vehicles into robotics and embodied AI. XPENG, a Chinese EV manufacturer founded in 2014, has leveraged its expertise in electric drivetrains, AI software, and autonomous systems to develop robotic platforms capable of dynamic movement and real-time environmental interaction. Humanoid robots like IRON rely on advanced motion planning algorithms, electric actuators, and sensor fusion systems - typically combining cameras, LiDAR, inertial measurement units (IMUs), and force sensors. These systems allow the robot to maintain balance, adjust posture, and perform coordinated movements that appear fluid and human-like. Modern humanoid locomotion depends heavily on real-time feedback control. Small positional corrections are made hundreds of times per second to stabilize joints and prevent falls. This is similar to the control architecture used in self-balancing robots and autonomous vehicles. XPENG’s broader robotics initiative aligns with a global push toward general-purpose humanoid platforms - machines designed to operate in human environments rather than factory-only settings. While still in early development stages, such robots are being researched for applications ranging from logistics and manufacturing to service roles and human-robot interaction studies. Robot plays "The Butterfly Lovers" on the erhu | 二胡 | 梁祝 | 乐器 The Erhu is a traditional Chinese bowed string instrument. It originated in the Tang Dynasty, with its predecessor being the "Xiqin" played by northern ethnic minorities. Although its structure is simple — a wooden sound box covered with python skin at the front, a neck standing upright on it, and two strings sounded by a bow — it possesses great acoustic wisdom. The timbre of the Erhu closely resembles the human voice, capable of vividly expressing emotions such as joy, anger, sorrow, and happiness.#robot #robotics #erhu #music #future

I spent days teaching a 3D-printed robot duck to walk. Most of that time, it was falling over. It’s my own build of the Open Duck Mini. The open-source, BDX-inspired biped created by Antoine Pirrone. The whole thing is 3D-printed and runs on hobby-grade servos instead of industrial actuators, which is what makes it buildable on a normal budget and also what makes it so hard to get walking. The hard part wasn’t the printing or the assembly. It was the sim-to-real gap. A gait that walks perfectly in MuJoCo hits real-world joint slop, servo lag, and a center of mass that won’t sit still, and just before you know it, the duck face plants into the floor. It took me 40+ calibration passes before it could take three steps without tipping! What the build came down to: • 3D-printed chassis • Per-joint offset calibration (where most of the pain lived) • Policy training in simulation (MuJoCo / Isaac Lab) • Build guide + docs via Tnkr • A lot of failed walks Real hardware. Real failures. Real progress.
